body_markdown:
Over 1700 vehicles will cross the block during[the Mecum Nashville 2026 sale](https://www.mecum.com/auctions/nashville-2026/lots/) , which will take place from September 22 to 26. The auction catalog includes something for everyone, from budget-friendly classics to modern hypercars with four-digit horsepower and seven-digit price tags, but the rare and unusual cars caught our attention as we looked through the lots.


You can find a split-window VW Bus, a 1960s Corvette, and a resto-modded SUV at just about every big-name auction. They’re cool, but they’re fairly common. What you don’t normally see in auction catalogs are one-off prototypes, limited-run Japanese-market SUVs, and French vans that are as small as they are eccentric. And yet, these are all part of the Mecum Nashville 2026 catalog.


Here are five of the coolest oddities that will be looking for a new home later this month.


## **1964 Plymouth Barracuda Landau Prototype**


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


[Lot S235](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1173284/1964-plymouth-barracuda-landau-prototype/?aa_id=785223-0)


The original[Plymouth Barracuda](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/1964-1966-barracudas-are-finally-getting-their-due/) , released in 1964, was exclusively available as a fastback, and a convertible wasn’t offered until the second-generation model landed in showrooms. The first-gen range would have looked different if this Landau Prototype had reached production. It was created by Chrysler designers to prove that a convertible Barracuda could work, but it wasn’t fitted with a full folding roof. Instead, it used a targa-like removable roof panel reminiscent of what Chevrolet has offered on the Corvette for the past few generations. Reasons why designers would have chosen this layout include structural rigidity, safety, and sheer simplicity.


Finished in gold over gold, this rare prototype is powered by a 273-cubic-inch V-8 linked to a push-button automatic transmission. It’s an enigmatic car, but what’s clear is that it hasn’t spent the past 60 years collecting dust in a warehouse: Its five-digit odometer shows about 52,500 miles. It’s fitted with an AM radio and a three-spoke steering wheel, among other period-correct equipment.


## **1978 Willam Fourgonnette**


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


[Lot T29](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1175204/1978-willam-fourgonnette/?aa_id=796840-0)


What the heck is a Willam? Good question; The company isn’t exactly a household name, even across the pond.


The brand was founded in 1967 by Henri Willame, who was the head of scooter manufacturer Lambretta, in a bid to revive[the microcar segment](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/valuation/with-microcars-on-the-rise-weird-and-wacky-is-the-name-of-the-game/) . He teamed up with an Italian industrialist named Carlo Lavezzari and set up a factory near Brescia, Italy, to build cars that were aimed at the French market. Willam’s unique breed of cars blurred the line between a scooter and a car: They were cheap, tiny, and unspeakably slow. The trade-off is that they could be driven by anyone holding a valid scooter license.


Willam built several different models, including an open-top Jeep CJ-like car called Farmer, a city car appropriately named City, and a commercial two-seater van named Fourgonnette. Mecum is auctioning off a 1978 example of the Fourgonnette that’s powered by a 125-cc, 5.6-horsepower single-cylinder scooter engine and a four-speed manual transmission. It’s painted yellow with a black bench seat, and there are no rear seats, so it should be more practical than its pocket-sized dimensions suggest.


## **1990 RMA Amphi-Ranger 2800 SR**


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


[Lot S347](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1177393/1990-rma-amphi-ranger-2800-sr/?aa_id=803633-0)


Germany’s best-known civilian amphibious car is[the Amphicar](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/amphicar-770-when-double-duty-did-not-trippel-the-fun/) , which was developed largely as a leisure vehicle. There’s another, heavier-duty amphibious model that wears a “made in Germany” label: The rare RMA Amphi-Ranger. RMA stands for Rheinhauer Maschinen und Armaturenbau, and the company specialized in manufacturing pipeline-related equipment such as valves, couplers, and adapters. It needed a car that it could drive out to pipelines for repairs, but it couldn’t find one that fit the bill, so it built its own.


RMA started from scratch. Released in 1985, the Amphi-Ranger featured a chassis made with galvanized steel and an aluminum body. Several engine options were available, including V-6s borrowed from Ford, and locking differentials made the Amphi-Ranger equally capable on land and on water. RMA realized that it had created something unique and began offering the SUV to the public in Germany and abroad, though sales were low. One of its biggest customers was the German police, who used the model to patrol the Rhine River. Production ended in 1995, largely because low demand made the model uneconomical to build.


The example in the Mecum Nashville 2026 sale is one of about 66 units sold, and it’s the only one believed to be located in the United States. Put another way, you’ll need to look across the pond if you want to find another one (though there’s no guarantee you’ll be able to sail it across the pond). It’s powered by the Ford-sourced 2.9-liter V-6 linked to a five-speed manual transmission on land. When you reach the water, you can use a switch on the dashboard to lower the rear-mounted propeller and keep going.


## **1998 Mitsubishi Pajero Junior Flying Pug**

[Lot T281](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1175447/1998-mitsubishi-pajero-jr-flying-pug/?aa_id=800165-0)


Enthusiasts often associate[the Mitsubishi Montero](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/all-new-mitsubishi-pajero-looks-capable-but-will-we-get-it-stateside/) (which is sold as the Pajero in global markets) with off-roading. It’s a rugged, body-on-frame SUV, and it has[won the grueling Paris-Dakar Rally](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/1985-dakar-winning-mitsubishi-pajero-restored/) several times, so this reputation is well-earned. There’s another side to the nameplate: In the 1990s, the full-size Pajero unexpectedly shared its name and image with a small, retro-styled SUV.


Known as the Pajero Junior Flying Pug, the model wore a full body kit inspired by 1950s British cars. The look added an upright front end with round headlights and a bright grille, a two-piece front bumper, a hood ornament, and round rear lights. Wheel arch flares that stuck out from the body added a finishing touch that ensured this Pajero turned heads everywhere it went.


While aftermarket brands[like Mitsuoka](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/mitsuoka-celebrates-55-years-of-replicas-with-civic-based-oddball/) have been giving Japanese-market cars a retro look for over two decades, the Flying Pug was designed in-house by Mitsubishi. The company planned to build 1000 units between September 1997 and June 1998, but it only managed to sell about 139, which makes this restyled SUV rarer than many hypercars. The example headed to the Mecum Nashville 2026 sale features a 79-horsepower, 1.0-liter four-cylinder engine, a three-speed automatic, and four-wheel drive.


## **2006 Pontiac Roush Signature G6**


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions


Mecum Auctions

[Lot S170](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1173889/2006-pontiac-roush-signature-g6/?aa_id=785443-0)


Pontiac made[a great deal of desirable cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/most-expensive-pontiacs-sold-at-auction/) over the years, including the GTO, the Firebird Trans Am, and[the G8](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-g8-was-pontiacs-last-model-and-inarguably-one-of-its-best/) , but the G6 is not often praised as one of its greatest hits. Mecum has found an exception to this rule: It’s auctioning a one-of-a-kind Roush Signature G6 that was built by Roush and unveiled at SEMA 2004. Designing a G6 worthy of the SEMA show required making numerous modifications.


Currently part of Roush’s own collection, the G6 is powered by a 3.5-liter V-6 with a cold-air intake and a GM Performance dual exhaust system. It doesn’t sound like the engine is drastically more powerful than stock, but it’s the styling that earned this G6 the GM Design Award at SEMA. It’s finished in Merles Opus Orange Yellow, it rides on black-finished 19-inch alloy wheels, and it wears a muscular-looking body kit that includes a deeper front bumper, more sculpted side skirts, and a trunk-mounted spoiler. The Roush Signature G6 rides lower than a run-of-the-mill, Hertz rental car-spec G6 thanks to a set of Eibach lowering springs.


Inside, Roush added Sparco front seats upholstered in black and yellow as well as Sparco-inspired rear seats. There are two auxiliary gauges (one for the engine oil pressure and one for the coolant temperature) on the driver-side A-pillar. All told, this G6 embodies many of the tuning trends that characterized the first half of the 2000s, and that’s a big part of its appeal. This is a rare chance to own a one-off car that you may have read about when you were flipping through car magazines two decades ago.
